newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - US rates, Russia, Korea lead.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - US rates, Russia, Korea lead.

text.p: The U.S. interest rate story will dominate investors' horizons this week while Russian politics and the implications for South Korea of a weakening yen spell a hectic week for global emerging markets.

"It's going to be a bit of a nervous week until we get the (U.S.) employment report out of the way," said Nigel Rendell, global emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel, pointing to a swathe of U.S. data including the purchasing managers survey and employment figures due out this week.

Investors will be watching them closely to see whether they give ammunition to the argument for a U.S. interest rate rise following indications of a more hawkish view last week from U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
ARGENTINA, given the peso-dollar peg, and MEXICO due to the importance of its exports to the United States, will be first in line to suffer from expectations of a U.S. interest rate rise.
"Greenspan wants to raise rates and his excuse for not raising them seems to be diminishing -- the employment report may just give him the incentive (he needs)," Rendell added.

"Already this week people have become nervous on Argentina, the Brady bonds have suffered and the equity market suffered a bit yesterday," he added. "And the slower the U.S. economy grows the worse it is for exporters in Mexico."
But Foreign & Colonial said that longer term these economies would be more resilient than in the past due to their stronger fundamentals and attractive valuations.

In eastern Europe RUSSIA will return to centre stage with market players bracing themselves for a cabinet reshuffle expected next week. It is likely to follow President Boris Yeltsin's state of the nation address on Thursday, which investors will scrutinise as much for evidence of Yeltsin's state of health as for word on the economy.
"He can't bluff his way through a 30 or 40 minute speech," said one Russian equity trader.
Fears Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin may be dismissed receded late last week though rumours persist that Defence Minister Igor Rodionov may be sacrificed in a likely reshuffle.
However Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analysts downplayed the implications of any such change.
"A pointer towards any reshuffle being a change of faces, not of underlying policy, is that there is absolutely no mention of replacing Sergei Dubinin as head of the central bank," they said.
Russian equities, whose ascendency so far this year has started to slow, are likely to rally on a strong presidential performance, dealers said.
Investors are also starting to evaluate the impact on Asian economies of a weakening Japanese yen.

Foreign & Colonial analysts said the weakness would cause an improvement in the current account deficits of investment-led economies such as MALAYSIA, THAILAND and INDONESIA but the news was less good for KOREA.

"The falling yen is obviously positive for Japanese competitiveness which, whilst a mild negative for the rest of the region, is a major blow for Korea, which is a direct competitor to Japan across the export sector," they said.
"The only answer is to depreciate alongside the yen, but this increases the debt burden on Korean companies with dollar-denominated borrowings, putting further pressure on margins."
Profit-taking in the stock markets of POLAND and the CZECH REPUBLIC towards the end of last week looks likely to continue, this week market players said.
In the Czech Republic this is being fuelled by a weakening currency as demand for the crown, which was strong in January due to a series of corporate Eurobond issues, slows down, Rendell said.
"The currency is coming under pressure and people are taking money out of the equity market -- I wouldn't be surprised if that continues this week," he said.
The Polish stock market on the other hand is entering a period of consolidation after its strength over the past two to three months.

Emerging equity market investors will be waiting for news likely on Monday of whether Washington has decided to certify Colombia as a partner in its anti-narcotics war this year after its decertification last year.
Markets breathed a sigh of relief last Friday when Mexico received its certification, without which could result in trade sanctions and the withholding of U.S. aid.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was up 0.1 percent at 331.71 points on Friday compared with a week ago.
Latin America was up 0.3 percent week on week at 629.69, Asia was down 0.2 percent at 267.82, and Europe, Middle East and Africa were up 0.4 percent at 160.83.
